newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Killer brain disease may be passed on by blood - WHO.
newsitem.headline: Killer brain disease may be passed on by blood - WHO.

text.p: The human form of mad cow disease can be transmitted by blood transfusion and people at risk from the fatal brain-wasting disorder must not donate blood, international experts declared on Wednesday.
A specialist committee of the World Health Organisation endorsed a warning by a leading U.S. scientist and ordered it sent to WHO's 191 member states.

Paul Brown of the National Institute of Health in Bethesda, Maryland, reported to WHO that he had injected the brains of healthy mice with blood from mice infected with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease or CJD.

Brown told reporters his experiments showed blood plasma could transmit the disease agent and this would also apply to the new variant of CJD thought to be derived from mad cow disease -- BSE or bovine spongiform encephalopathy.
He said the risk was small, but still existed and singled out three high-risk groups who should not be allowed to donate blood:
- Members of families in which CJD has been caused by genetic mutation. "Members of such families should not donate blood because a certain number of them are going to die from CJD," Brown said.
- People who received growth hormones in the early 1980s. A proportion of these people have already died from CJD because they received contaminated growth hormones and deaths are continuing.
- Neurosurgery patients whose doctors took transplants from corpses that died of CJD.

Brown said the outer brain covering known as "dura mater" was still being used in neurosurgery transplants and other operations such as replacement of eardrums and intestinal surgery and that this had to be stopped.

"In view of transmissions of CJD using this substance, and view of the possibility of using alternative materials, the working group recommended that this material, dura mater, should not be used for any purpose in the future," he said.
